key_terms.meaning: The four linked views a manager balances: people, product, process, project.
A number about the way work is done (defect removal rate, review hours per page, rework %) used to judge process improvement.
A number about the delivered software itself (size in LOC or function points, defects per KLOC, cyclomatic number, reliability).
A size measure counted from inputs, outputs, queries, files and interfaces, independent of the language used.
Constructive Cost Model: E = a × (KLOC)^b person-months, where E is effort, KLOC is thousands of lines of code, and a and b depend on project class (organic, semi-detached, embedded).
One person working full time for one month; total effort is PM = number of people × months they work.
A tree that splits the product into tasks small enough to estimate, assign and schedule.
The longest-duration path through the task network; it fixes the shortest possible project duration and has zero float.
A bar chart with calendar time across and tasks down, showing start, end and overlap of each task.
RE = probability × impact; the expected loss if a risk occurs, used to rank risks.
Action taken before the risk hits so that its probability or its impact is reduced.
Watching the risk indicators during the project so the plan is triggered when needed.
Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management plan: one written page per risk with trigger, actions and owner.
A risk that the delivered software will be wrong or poor: low quality, late delivery, scope creep.
A formally reviewed and agreed version of a work product; changes to it need an approved change request.
Any work product placed under configuration control: code file, SRS, test plan, build script, design model.
A structured meeting of peers that examines a work product against a checklist and records defects found.
The most formal review: fixed roles, entry criteria, preparation with checklists, defect log and exit criteria.
Changing working software to add features or improve performance and maintainability at user request.
Written steps to restore the previous release in production if the new one fails, with a time limit for the decision.

takeaways: People, product, process and project are not four separate jobs; the plan is where all four meet.
A measurement is useful only when it changes a decision, so pick few metrics and define them once.
Decomposition gives an estimate you can defend task by task; an empirical model gives a fast cross-check.
The critical path controls the finish date; adding people to a late critical task can make it later, not earlier.
Risk management is cheap when done early and impossible when done after the risk has hit.
A baseline is a promise: nothing changes in it without a recorded, approved request.
Reviews find defects at the stage where they are cheapest to fix, which is before any test runs.
Maintenance is not one activity but four, and preventive maintenance is what keeps the other three from growing.
Re-engineering is chosen when the yearly cost of patching exceeds the one-time cost of rebuilding, not because the code is old.
A release is a decision, not a copy: version, test in staging, ship with a rollback plan, then record it.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on structure: define the term, give the standard model or formula with every symbol explained, then apply it to the numbers in the question.

bank.q: Explain the four Ps of the management spectrum and show how each one feeds into a single project plan.
outline: Name the four Ps: people, product, process, project
One paragraph on each with what the manager decides there
Show the link: product scope sets tasks, process sets activities, people set capacity, project is the plan that joins them
Example of a decision that needs all four together

bank.q: Distinguish process metrics from product metrics. Give three examples of each and state the question each metric answers.
outline: Definition of measurement, metric and indicator
Process metrics with examples: defect removal efficiency, review rate, rework percentage
Product metrics with examples: KLOC, defects per KLOC, mean time to failure
Why process metrics guide improvement and product metrics guide acceptance

bank.q: Explain the COCOMO model: its three product classes, the basic effort equation and the duration equation, defining every symbol.
outline: Organic, semi-detached, embedded and when each applies
E = a × (KLOC)^b with E in person-months and KLOC in thousands of delivered lines
D = c × E^d with D in months
Limitations: estimate depends on size estimate and on constants fitted to past projects

bank.q: Define a software risk. Distinguish process risk, product risk and technology risk with one example of each.
outline: Risk as a possible future loss with a probability and an impact
Process risk example: staff turnover or unrealistic schedule
Product risk example: poor quality or scope creep
Technology risk example: an unfamiliar framework or an unproven database
Why risks are written down, not remembered

bank.q: What is software configuration management? List its main activities and the role of a baseline in each.
outline: Identification of configuration items
Version control and check-in/check-out
Change control through a change request and approval board
Configuration audit and status reporting
Baseline as the approved reference point

bank.q: A module is estimated at 32 KLOC and is of organic type with a = 2.4, b = 1.05, c = 2.5, d = 0.38. Compute effort in person-months and nominal duration in months, and state the average team size.
outline: E = 2.4 × 32^1.05 ≈ 91 person-months
Average staff = E ÷ D ≈ 6.5, so about 6 to 7 people
Comment that the KLOC figure must be a careful estimate, not a guess

bank.q: For a six-task project with given durations and dependencies, draw the activity network, find the critical path and project duration, and compute the total float of one non-critical task.
outline: Forward pass for earliest start and finish of every task
Backward pass for latest start and finish
Identify tasks with zero float and the path through them
State project duration as the earliest finish of the last task
Float of a non-critical task = latest start minus earliest start

bank.q: Five risks are listed with their probabilities and impact in person-months. Compute risk exposure for each, rank them, and write the RMMM entries for the top two.
outline: RE = probability × impact, shown as a small table
Ranking by RE value and a threshold above which a risk gets a plan
Each RMMM entry: trigger or indicator, mitigation action, monitoring method, management contingency, owner
Note that probability and impact must be re-estimated at each milestone

bank.q: A developer asks to change a module that is already baselined. Describe the full SCM sequence you would follow and the records produced.
outline: Change request raised with reason and affected items
Impact analysis on cost, schedule and other items
Approval or rejection by the change control authority
Check-out, edit, check-in with a new version number
Regression test, re-baseline, update status log and audit trail

bank.q: You must ship a new version of a three-tier web application. Write the release plan: version numbering, staging checks, deployment steps and rollback plan.
outline: Version scheme: major, minor, patch and what each change means
Staging environment that mirrors production; database migration tested there
Deployment order of components and the freeze window
Health checks and smoke tests after go-live
Rollback triggers, time limit, and how data changes are reversed

bank.q: A bank runs a twelve-year-old transaction system. Compare corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive maintenance for it, and recommend either continued maintenance or re-engineering with justification.
outline: Define the four maintenance types with a bank example for each
Cost and risk of each option
Signs favouring re-engineering: rising patch cost, missing documentation, hard dependency on retired platform
Reverse engineering and restructuring as a middle path
Decision rule based on yearly maintenance cost versus rebuild cost, and on business risk

bank.q: A project has a full schedule, a complete task list and a working estimation model, yet it fails. Using measurement and risk management, explain how this is possible.
outline: Schedule without measurement gives no early warning
Metrics that were collected but not acted on
Unranked risks and no trigger conditions
Risk projection done once at start and never refreshed
Link between process metrics, defect trends and schedule slippage
Corrective step: review checkpoints tied to metric thresholds and risk indicators

bank.q: Compare technical reviews with testing as defect-removal methods. Which defect classes does each catch better, and why are reviews cheaper when done early?
outline: What a review examines: any work product, not just executable code
Testing can only reveal failures of executed paths
Cost of a defect rises with the stage where it is found
Review types: informal, walkthrough, inspection, with roles and checklists
Limitations of reviews: no performance proof, needs preparation time and trained moderators
Practical mix: reviews on requirements and design, testing for behaviour

bank.q: A team of eight people has a fixed delivery date and a first estimate that is 40 percent above the available effort. Using estimation, scheduling, risk and release planning, set out how you would handle the situation.
outline: Check the size estimate first with a second method such as function points
Re-decompose and look for tasks that can be cut or moved to a later release
Compress schedule only where the critical path allows; note that adding people to the critical path can delay it
Record the reduced scope as a risk in the RMMM plan with trigger and owner
Agree a first release that ships a working subset, with a version number and rollback plan
Report residual risk to stakeholders in writing

glossary.def: Fixing defects found in software that is already in use.
Changing working software so it keeps working after a change in its environment, such as a new operating system or tax rule.
Adding features or improving performance and maintainability at the user's request.
Changing software that still works, to stop future defects, for example by restructuring a fragile module or adding checks.
Rebuilding an existing system, usually starting from reverse engineering, to improve its structure without changing what it does.
Reading existing code and data to recover design and requirements information that was never documented.
An informal review where the author leads colleagues through a work product and they ask questions.
A formal review with defined roles, checklists, preparation time, a defect log and exit criteria.
The person who plans and runs a review meeting, keeps it on the product and not on the author.
The review team member who writes down every defect found, but does not suggest fixes during the meeting.
The set of planned process activities, standards, reviews and audits that give confidence the product will meet its quality goals.
The discipline of identifying work products, controlling their versions and approving their changes.
The small group that approves or rejects change requests against a baseline.
A tool and practice that records every saved change to a file and lets any earlier version be recovered.
Estimating the probability and the impact of each identified risk so risks can be ranked.
Breaking a broad risk into smaller, checkable conditions and attaching a measurable indicator to each.
Identifying risks before they occur and acting on them; the reactive strategy waits for the problem and then fires.
Asking several experts to estimate separately and anonymously, then repeating until the estimates converge.
Splitting the whole product or job into smaller parts that can each be estimated, assigned and tracked.
A size measure counting delivered source lines; KLOC means thousands of lines.
A network diagram of tasks and their dependencies, used to find the critical path.
Comparing planned cost of work scheduled, actual cost spent and planned cost of work completed to show schedule and cost health.
A copy of the production setup where a release is tested before real users see it.
A numbering scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where the major number rises for incompatible changes and the patch number for backward-compatible fixes.
